lessons.title: Allah's names and attributes: the methodology of Ahl as-Sunnah
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we say something is real if we cannot say how it is?
objectives: To understand the method Ahl as-Sunnah use to affirm Allah's names and attributes
successCriteria: All: state the principle of 42:11
Most: explain the four errors avoided with an example of each

keywords.def: those who follow the Sunnah and the Companions

hook.text: How can we say something is real if we cannot say how it is?
hook.a: We know Allah hears and sees because He told us; the 'how' is beyond us, and we do not invent it.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing' (ash-Shura 42:11).

teach.heading: Four errors
teach.note: Each error with a simple example.

check.q: 'Allah hears, but not like creation hears' avoids ...
check.why: It affirms (no ta'til) and denies likeness (no tamthil).

practice.q: Give an example of each error and correct it.
practice.a: Tahrif: 'His hand means power only' corrected to affirming as fits His majesty; etc.
practice.model: Teacher does ta'til: 'Saying Allah does not truly see denies 42:11's "the Seeing". Correct: Allah truly sees, not like us.'

independent.q: Stretch: why did the Salaf say the 'how' is unknown but the meaning is known?
independent.a: The meaning is clear Arabic; the reality of Allah's attributes is beyond us

exit.q: Takyif means ...

exit.a: Yes: Allah told us it is real; the how is beyond us

lessons.title: The Akhirah: death, the grave and the barzakh
lessons.bigQuestion: If you knew your exams were tomorrow you would prepare tonight. Why do people prepare less for something certain like death?
objectives: To understand what Muslims believe happens at death and in the grave, and why it matters now
successCriteria: All: state three beliefs about death and the grave
Most: explain the questioning in the grave with evidence
Some: explain how belief in the grave shapes a Muslim's choices
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: life as preparation; Moral: accountability

keywords.def: the barrier: life in the grave until the Day of Resurrection
a person's fixed term of life

hook.text: If you knew your exams were tomorrow you would prepare tonight. Why do people prepare less for something certain like death?
hook.a: Because the date is unknown; Islam teaches us to prepare every day.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Every soul will taste death, and you will only be given your full reward on the Day of Resurrection' (Al 'Imran 3:185).

starter.q: Bismillah. Ar-Raqib means ...
39:53 tells us not to despair of ...

quote.text: كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ذَائِقَةُ المَوْتِ

teach.heading: The grave
bullets: About the Prophet ﷺ and faith
teach.note: The questioning about 'this man', the Prophet ﷺ, is reported by Anas in Bukhari. Allah says He keeps firm those who believe with the firm word in this world and the Hereafter (Ibrahim 14:27).

teach.heading: The barzakh
bullets: Deeds cannot be added, except ongoing charity
teach.note: Al-Mu'minun 23:100 mentions the barzakh. Ongoing charity, beneficial knowledge and a righteous child's du'a continue (Muslim).

check.q: Which three things continue after death (Muslim)?

check.why: Hadith in Muslim.

practice.q: Explain the questioning in the grave with evidence.
practice.a: Two angels question the person about the Prophet ﷺ (Bukhari, Anas); Allah makes believers firm (14:27)
practice.model: Teacher: 'Belief: the dead are questioned. Evidence: Bukhari's hadith of Anas and 14:27. Meaning: firmness comes from living by iman now.'

independent.q: Extended answer in the portal response box (or a Forms long-answer question): 'How should belief in death and the grave affect the way a Muslim lives?' Two developed points with evidence and a conclusion.

independent.model: Teacher writes point 1: 'Because the ajal is unknown, a Muslim repents quickly. For example, ...'

independent.q: Stretch: what is sadaqah jariyah and give two modern examples?
independent.a: Ongoing charity: a well, a masjid, a beneficial app or book

exit.q: Barzakh means ...
exit.a: The barrier: life in the grave
options: The barrier: life in the grave

exit.q: Back to our ponder: why prepare less for death?
exit.a: The date is unknown; Islam says prepare every day

lessons.title: Al-Qadr: divine decree and human responsibility

objectives: To understand belief in al-Qadr and why it does not remove human responsibility
successCriteria: All: name the four levels of qadr
Most: explain why people are still responsible for their choices
Some: respond to the argument 'if it is written, why try?' with evidence
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: trust in Allah; Moral: responsibility for choices

hook.text: If Allah already knows what you will choose, are you still free to choose? Discuss.
hook.a: Yes: Allah's knowledge does not force us; we choose and are responsible, and Allah knows what we will choose.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Act, for each person will be eased towards what he was created for', then recited al-Layl 92:5-10 (Bukhari and Muslim).

starter.q: Bismillah. 99:7-8 is about ...
starter.a: An atom's weight of good and evil

starter.q: Which ayah: no soul will be wronged?
Mizan means ...

teach.heading: The sixth pillar
bullets: Believe in qadar, its good and its bad
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah.

teach.heading: Four levels
teach.note: A summary scholars give from the Qur'an and Sunnah.
cycle: Mashi'ah: nothing happens unless Allah wills

teach.heading: Choice and responsibility
bullets: We are judged on our choices
teach.note: Allah says: 'And you do not will except that Allah wills' (at-Takwir 81:29): we will, within His will.

teach.heading: 'Then why act?'
bullets: 'Act, each is eased to what he was created for'
teach.note: Bukhari and Muslim (from 'Ali).

check.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ answer when asked 'why act if it is written'?
options: Act, for each is eased to what he was created for
check.why: Bukhari and Muslim; then 92:5-10.

practice.q: Explain why people are still responsible.
practice.a: Allah gave us will and choice; His knowledge does not force us; we are judged on what we choose
practice.model: Teacher: 'A teacher may predict a lazy pupil will fail; the prediction does not cause the failure. Allah's knowledge is perfect, but it does not force us.' (an analogy, with limits: Allah's knowledge is not a guess)

independent.q: Extended answer in the portal response box (or a Forms long-answer question): 'If everything is decreed, people cannot be held responsible for their actions.' Evaluate (12-mark style) using the hadith in Bukhari and Muslim, 92:5-10 and 81:29.
independent.a: Against: choice, the hadith, 92:5-10; For: misunderstood fatalism; judgement: disagree
independent.model: Teacher writes the 'against' opening: 'Most Muslims would disagree, because the Prophet ﷺ told the Companions to act (Bukhari and Muslim).'

independent.q: Stretch: why is the teacher's prediction analogy limited?
independent.a: Allah's knowledge is perfect and He created everything; no analogy fully fits

exit.q: Kitabah means ...
Back to our ponder: are you free to choose?
exit.a: Yes, and responsible; Allah knows what we will choose

lessons.unit: Spring 1: The Prophet as leader and sawm
lessons.title: The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah: the journey and the pledge
lessons.bigQuestion: Why might 1,400 people set out to visit Makkah carrying no weapons for war, even though Makkah was hostile?
objectives: To understand why the Prophet ﷺ set out for Makkah in 6 AH and what happened at Hudaybiyyah before the treaty
successCriteria: All: describe the journey and its peaceful purpose
Most: explain the rumour about Uthman and the pledge under the tree
Some: explain what Bay'at ar-Ridwan shows about the Companions' faith
lessons.crossCurricular: History: diplomacy and negotiation between rival powers
lessons.smsc: Moral: seeking peace and honouring commitments

keywords.def: a place near Makkah where the treaty was agreed in 6 AH
the pledge under the tree that pleased Allah (48:18)
the sacred state and clothing for pilgrimage
animals brought to be sacrificed at Makkah

hook.text: Why might 1,400 people set out to visit Makkah carrying no weapons for war, even though Makkah was hostile?
hook.a: They came for 'umrah, in peace: ihram and sacrificial animals showed they wanted worship, not war.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree' (al-Fath 48:18).

starter.q: In which year was the Battle of Badr?
What is 'umrah?
Who led Quraysh at Badr and was killed there?
In which year CE was the Hijrah?

teach.heading: Setting out for 'umrah
bullets: In ihram, with animals for sacrifice
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Dhul Qa'dah is a sacred month when fighting was forbidden by Arab custom. Ask: what signals of peace can you see?

teach.heading: Stopped at Hudaybiyyah
bullets: His camel al-Qaswa' knelt and would not move
'The One who held back the elephant held her back'
He would accept any plan that honoured Allah's sanctities
teach.note: Bukhari's long narration: the Prophet ﷺ said he would agree to any plan from Quraysh that respected the sanctity of Allah's House. Link to Surah al-Fil and the Year of the Elephant.

teach.heading: Messengers and the pledge
teach.note: Quraysh sent envoys including Urwah ibn Mas'ud, who reported that he had seen kings but never people honour a leader as the Companions honoured Muhammad ﷺ (Bukhari). Uthman was sent into Makkah; a false rumour said he had been killed; the Companions pledged under a tree not to flee. Uthman returned safely.

timeline.text: Camp at Hudaybiyyah; Quraysh block the way
Envoys go back and forth (Urwah ibn Mas'ud)
Uthman returns; Suhayl ibn Amr sent to agree terms

teach.heading: Why the pledge matters
bullets: Ready to stand firm, yet seeking peace
teach.note: Those present at the pledge (ahl ash-shajarah) are honoured; the Prophet ﷺ said none of those who gave the pledge under the tree would enter the Fire (Muslim).

check.q: What made the Companions give the pledge under the tree?
options: A rumour that Uthman had been killed
They wanted to enter Makkah by force
check.why: The false rumour about Uthman led to the pledge to stand firm. There was no attack, and they had come for 'umrah, not to force entry.

practice.q: Give three pieces of evidence that the Muslims came in peace.
practice.a: Ihram; animals for sacrifice; the sacred month; only sheathed travellers' swords; the Prophet's ﷺ readiness to accept a plan that honoured the sanctities.
practice.model: I do the first: 'They wore ihram, the clothing of pilgrims, not armour.' Pupils add two more on whiteboards.

practice.q: Which ayah mentions the pledge under the tree?
practice.a: Al-Fath 48:18

practice.q: Who was sent into Makkah to negotiate?
practice.a: Uthman ibn Affan

independent.q: In the portal response box, write a PEEL paragraph: 'Explain why the Prophet ﷺ went to Makkah in 6 AH and how the Muslims showed peaceful intentions.'
independent.a: Point: to perform 'umrah. Evidence: ihram, hady, sacred month. Explain: they sought worship and peace. Link.
independent.model: Teacher models: 'Point: the Prophet ﷺ set out to perform 'umrah, not to fight. Evidence: about 1,400 Companions travelled in ihram with animals for sacrifice in the sacred month of Dhul Qa'dah. Explain: ...'

independent.q: Extend: what did Urwah ibn Mas'ud's report tell Quraysh?
independent.a: That the Companions' love and respect for the Prophet ﷺ was unlike anything he had seen, even with kings.

independent.q: Stretch: why do you think Allah praised the pledge in the Qur'an?
independent.a: It showed sincere loyalty and readiness to sacrifice for Allah at a moment of fear (48:18).

exit.q: About how many Muslims went to Hudaybiyyah?
Back to our ponder: why come without weapons for war?
exit.a: They came for worship ('umrah) and wanted peace.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: The Prophet as leader and sawm
lessons.title: The Conquest of Makkah
lessons.bigQuestion: If you entered the city of people who had persecuted you for twenty years, and you now held the power, what would you do?
objectives: To understand how the Conquest of Makkah happened and what it shows about the Prophet's ﷺ leadership
successCriteria: All: sequence the main events of the conquest
Most: explain how bloodshed was avoided
Some: explain the significance of clearing the Ka'bah of idols
lessons.crossCurricular: History: how a city changed hands with almost no bloodshed
lessons.smsc: Moral: humility in success

keywords.def: the valley near Makkah where the army camped
leader of Quraysh who accepted Islam at the conquest

hook.text: If you entered the city of people who had persecuted you for twenty years, and you now held the power, what would you do?
hook.a: The Prophet ﷺ entered with his head lowered in humility, almost without fighting, and forgave.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest, and you see the people entering the religion of Allah in multitudes, then glorify the praises of your Lord and ask His forgiveness' (an-Nasr 110:1-3).

starter.q: Why was the treaty broken?
starter.a: Quraysh helped Banu Bakr attack Khuza'ah
options: Quraysh helped Banu Bakr attack Khuza'ah

starter.q: Which ayah calls Hudaybiyyah a clear victory?
About how many marched to Makkah in 8 AH?
Name the four terms of the treaty.
starter.a: Ten-year truce; 'umrah next year; one-way return of people; free alliances

teach.heading: The march
bullets: Plans kept secret to avoid a battle
Camp at Marr az-Zahran: many campfires
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. The large army and the campfires were meant to make fighting pointless so that Makkah would surrender peacefully.

teach.heading: Abu Sufyan and safety
bullets: Abu Sufyan came out and accepted Islam
Safe: whoever enters Abu Sufyan's house
Safe: whoever stays home with the door shut
teach.note: The three declarations of safety are reported in Muslim. They gave every Makkan an easy way to be safe. Only one column (under Khalid ibn al-Walid) met brief resistance.

teach.heading: Entering Makkah
teach.note: Bukhari (from Ibn Mas'ud) reports that he struck the idols around the Ka'bah reciting 17:81. Seerah reports describe his humility on entering and Bilal giving the adhan from the Ka'bah. Never show the Prophet ﷺ in images.

timeline.text: Enters with head lowered in humility
Bilal gives the adhan from the Ka'bah

teach.heading: Why it matters
bullets: The Ka'bah returned to tawhid, as Ibrahim built it
teach.note: Link to Ibrahim and Isma'il building the House for the worship of Allah alone (2:127). Surah an-Nasr tells the Prophet ﷺ to respond to victory with praise and seeking forgiveness.

check.q: What did Allah command the Prophet ﷺ to do at the time of victory (110:3)?
options: Glorify Allah's praise and seek forgiveness
check.why: Surah an-Nasr commands praise and istighfar: humility, not pride or revenge.

practice.q: Explain how the three declarations of safety helped avoid bloodshed.
practice.a: They gave every Makkan a simple way to be safe (Abu Sufyan's house, staying home, the Masjid), so few people fought.
practice.model: I do: 1) List the three places. 2) Ask: could ordinary people easily reach one? Yes. 3) So most stayed safe and did not fight. 4) This shows mercy and wise planning.

practice.q: Which ayah did he recite while removing the idols?
Who gave the adhan from the Ka'bah?
practice.a: Bilal

independent.q: In the portal response box, write a news report 'Makkah opens its gates' (no pictures of people): headline, the march, the safety declarations, the idols, the reaction. Then one sentence on what it shows about the Prophet ﷺ.
independent.a: Accurate date, numbers, Abu Sufyan, three safe places, 360 idols and 17:81, Bilal, and a reflection on humility and mercy.
independent.model: Teacher writes the headline and first line: 'MAKKAH OPENS ITS GATES. In Ramadan of 8 AH, an army of about 10,000 arrived at Marr az-Zahran ...'

independent.q: Extend: why was removing the idols so significant?
independent.a: The Ka'bah was built for the worship of Allah alone; it was restored to tawhid.

independent.q: Stretch: compare the Prophet's ﷺ entry into Makkah with how conquerors usually behaved.
independent.a: Many conquerors took revenge or loot; he entered humbly and gave safety.

exit.q: In which month and year was Makkah conquered?
Back to our ponder: what did the Prophet ﷺ do with his power?
exit.a: Entered humbly, gave safety and forgave.

lessons.homework: Learn Surah an-Nasr (110) with its meaning and explain to someone at home how it links to the conquest.
lessons.send: SEND: event cards with place pictures. EAL: news report frame. Stretch: research Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl after the conquest.

Over a hundred thousand are reported to have joined

teach.heading: The journey of Hajj
teach.note: Order of key events.

lessons.title: Sawm: the rules of fasting
lessons.bigQuestion: Ramadan is about to begin. What do you need to know so that your fast is correct?
objectives: To understand the rules of fasting in Ramadan so that pupils can fast correctly
successCriteria: All: state who must fast and the times of the fast
Most: identify what breaks and does not break the fast
Some: explain qada' and fidyah and who each applies to
lessons.crossCurricular: Science (Year 9 biology): keeping the body hydrated and nourished at suhur and iftar
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: obedience to Allah in private

keywords.def: fasting from dawn to sunset with intention, for Allah
having reached adulthood in Islamic law
making up a missed fast later
feeding a poor person for each day when someone cannot fast at all

hook.text: Ramadan is about to begin. What do you need to know so that your fast is correct?
hook.a: Who must fast, the intention, what breaks the fast, who is excused and how to make up days.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'O you who believe, fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, so that you may attain taqwa' (al-Baqarah 2:183), and 'Allah intends ease for you, not hardship' (2:185).

starter.q: Which ayah praises the Prophet's ﷺ great character?
Ramadan is which month of the Islamic calendar?
In which month was the Qur'an first revealed?
What does taqwa mean?
starter.a: Awareness of Allah that leads to obedience

teach.heading: Who must fast?
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Children are encouraged to practise. Fasting is from true dawn (fajr) to sunset (maghrib) (2:187). The intention is made in the heart; the majority of scholars say it is made before fajr for each Ramadan fast.

teach.heading: Breaks the fast or not?
teach.note: Eating or drinking on purpose breaks the fast; so do deliberate vomiting and other acts scholars list. The Prophet ﷺ said whoever forgets and eats or drinks should complete the fast, for Allah fed him and gave him drink (Bukhari and Muslim).

cards: B. Drinking by mistake, having forgotten
C. Making yourself vomit on purpose
E. Showering or swimming without swallowing water
H. Tasting nothing but smelling food

teach.heading: Who is excused?
bullets: The ill and travellers: qada' later (2:184)
Women in their monthly period: qada' later
Pregnant or nursing mothers, as scholars explain
Those who can never fast: fidyah (2:184)
teach.note: Qada': make up each missed day before the next Ramadan. Fidyah: feed one poor person for each day, for the very elderly or permanently ill. Deliberately breaking a Ramadan fast without excuse is a serious sin; scholars explain what must be done to make up for it.

check.q: Hamza travels a long journey in Ramadan and does not fast for two days. What must he do?
check.why: Travellers make up the days (2:184). Fidyah is for those who can never fast.

teach.heading: Sunnahs of fasting
bullets: Eat suhur: there is blessing in it
Hasten to break the fast at sunset
Break it with dates or water
teach.note: Suhur and hastening iftar: Bukhari and Muslim. Dates or water: reported in Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi.

practice.q: Sara eats a biscuit at 3 pm, then remembers she is fasting. What is the ruling?
practice.a: Her fast is valid: she forgot. She stops eating when she remembers and continues fasting.
practice.model: I do: 1) Was it deliberate? No. 2) Evidence: whoever forgets and eats should complete the fast (Bukhari and Muslim). 3) Ruling: the fast is valid; stop and carry on.

practice.q: Who pays fidyah?
practice.a: Someone who can never fast, e.g. the very elderly

independent.q: Fiqh scenarios (pupil PDF), then explain each in the portal response box: a) Ali swims and swallows no water. b) Maryam has flu for three days. c) Grandad, 90, cannot fast at all. d) Yusuf drinks juice at noon on purpose.
independent.a: a) Valid. b) Excused: qada' three days later. c) Fidyah: feed a poor person for each day. d) Broken: sinful; repent and make it up, as scholars explain.
independent.model: Teacher does a): 'Swimming does not break the fast as long as no water is swallowed, so Ali's fast is valid.'

independent.q: Extend: why does Islam give exemptions from fasting?
independent.a: Islam is ease (2:185); fasting must not cause harm.

independent.q: Stretch: what is the difference between qada' and fidyah?
independent.a: Qada' is making up the day; fidyah is feeding the poor when making up is impossible.

exit.q: When does the fast end each day?
Back to our ponder: what do you need to know so your fast is correct?
exit.a: Who fasts, intention, what breaks it, exemptions, qada' and fidyah.

hook.text: Would you sign an agreement that looked unfair to your side? What might make it worth signing?
hook.a: If it brought peace and long-term benefit. The Prophet ﷺ accepted terms that looked unfair, trusting Allah.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'O you who believe, fulfil your contracts' (al-Ma'idah 5:1). The Prophet ﷺ kept the treaty's terms even when it was painful.

bullets: Ali wrote; Suhayl objected to the wording
The Prophet ﷺ accepted both changes
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Bukhari reports the changes. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'By Allah, I am the Messenger of Allah even if you deny me.' Ask: why would he accept this wording?

teach.heading: The terms
teach.note: Terms as reported in Bukhari and the seerah; the ten-year length is reported in the seerah and Abu Dawud.

head: Term
What it said
rows: Return now; come next year for three days

Any tribe may ally with either side

teach.heading: Abu Jandal
bullets: Suhayl's son arrived in chains, a Muslim
Suhayl demanded him back under the terms
The Prophet ﷺ kept the agreement
He told Abu Jandal to be patient: Allah would make a way
teach.note: Bukhari reports Abu Jandal's arrival. The treaty had just been agreed, so the Prophet ﷺ honoured it, though it was painful for everyone. Handle sensitively.

check.q: Why did the Prophet ﷺ return Abu Jandal?
options: To keep the agreed terms of the treaty
Because Abu Jandal was not a Muslim
Because Abu Jandal asked to go
check.why: He honoured the treaty (5:1). Abu Jandal was a Muslim and begged not to be returned; fear was not the reason.

teach.heading: The Companions' distress
bullets: Umar asked: 'Are we not upon the truth?'
The Prophet ﷺ: 'I will not disobey Him; He will help me'
Abu Bakr gave the same answer
teach.note: Bukhari: when the Companions were slow to shave and sacrifice, Umm Salamah advised the Prophet ﷺ to do it himself without speaking; when they saw him, they all followed. Umar later did good deeds to make up for his strong words.

practice.q: Which term seemed most unfair to the Muslims, and why?
practice.a: Term 3: Makkans joining the Muslims were returned, but Muslims joining Quraysh were not; it looked one-sided.
practice.model: I do: 1) Read each term. 2) Ask: is it equal for both sides? 3) Term 3 is not: it only works one way. 4) So it seemed most unfair.

practice.q: How long was the truce to last?
practice.a: Ten years

practice.q: Who advised the Prophet ﷺ to shave and sacrifice first?
practice.a: Umm Salamah

independent.q: In the portal response box, write Umar's diary entry for the day of the treaty: his worries, his questions, and what the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr told him. Start: 'Today the treaty was written ...'

independent.q: Extend: what does Umm Salamah's advice show about leadership?
independent.a: Actions persuade more than words; the leader acted first and the people followed.

independent.q: Stretch: why is keeping a promise to an enemy important in Islam?
independent.a: Allah commands fulfilling contracts (5:1); trustworthiness is part of iman, whoever the other side is.

exit.q: Which wording was changed in the treaty?

exit.a: Peace and long-term benefit, and trust in Allah's plan.

hook.text: Have you ever accepted something you did not like, and later realised it was good for you?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you, and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. Allah knows and you do not know' (al-Baqarah 2:216).

points: Quraysh recognised the Muslims as an equal party

teach.heading: Abu Basir
bullets: Escaped to Madinah; returned under the treaty
Escaped again and camped by the coast
Others joined him, raiding Quraysh caravans
Quraysh begged to cancel the third term
teach.note: Bukhari reports Abu Basir's story and that Abu Jandal joined him. Quraysh asked the Prophet ﷺ to take in those who came, so the term that looked worst for the Muslims ended at Quraysh's own request.

teach.heading: Patience and trust
bullets: The Prophet ﷺ trusted Allah's promise
The Companions obeyed despite their feelings
Allah confirmed the vision of entering Makkah (48:27)
teach.note: Al-Fath 48:27: Allah fulfilled the vision of His Messenger: you will enter al-Masjid al-Haram in safety. They did, the following year ('umrat al-qada').

teach.heading: Lessons for us
bullets: Short-term loss can bring long-term good
Obey Allah even when feelings resist
Peace can achieve more than war
teach.note: Ask pupils for a modern example of each (a disappointing exam result leading to a better path, keeping a promise to a sibling).

practice.q: Explain how the 'returning people' term turned out well for the Muslims.
practice.a: Abu Basir and others formed a group that hurt Quraysh's trade, so Quraysh asked for the term to be dropped.
practice.model: I do: 1) The term: Makkans who joined the Muslims were returned. 2) Abu Basir was returned but escaped and set up camp. 3) Others joined; they attacked caravans. 4) Quraysh asked the Prophet ﷺ to take them, ending the term.

practice.q: Which ayah teaches 'perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you'?

independent.q: In the portal response box: 'The terms of Hudaybiyyah were a defeat for the Muslims.' Write two paragraphs: one agreeing, one disagreeing, each with evidence.
independent.a: Agree: sent home, wording changed, one-sided term, Abu Jandal. Disagree: peace, recognition, Abu Basir ended the term, 48:27 vision fulfilled, 2:216.
independent.model: Teacher models the 'agree' paragraph start: 'Some would agree, because the Muslims had to return without performing 'umrah and accept that "Messenger of Allah" was removed. For example ...'

independent.q: Extend: how does Hudaybiyyah show tawakkul?
independent.a: The Prophet ﷺ did what Allah commanded and trusted the outcome to Him.

independent.q: Stretch: what does Umar's reaction teach about honest questions in faith?
independent.a: It is human to struggle; the answer is to seek understanding from the right source and then obey.

exit.q: What did Allah confirm in 48:27?
exit.a: The vision of entering al-Masjid al-Haram in safety
options: The vision of entering al-Masjid al-Haram in safety

exit.q: Back to our ponder: share a time you disliked something that turned out good.

lessons.homework: Write a short reflection: one situation in your life where 2:216 could help you be patient.
lessons.send: SEND: the compare table as cut-out cards. EAL: connectives for agree and disagree. Stretch: include 48:27 in your answer.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: The Prophet as leader and sawm
lessons.title: Hudaybiyyah: the results and 'a clear victory'
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a peace agreement be called a victory when no battle was won?
objectives: To understand why Allah called the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah a clear victory
successCriteria: All: name three results of the treaty
Most: use numbers to show how Islam spread during the truce
Some: explain how the treaty led to the conquest of Makkah
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: comparing quantities, the growth from about 1,400 to about 10,000 in two years
lessons.smsc: Social: how peace allows people to understand each other

keywords.def: an agreement to stop fighting for a time
a tribe allied to the Muslims

hook.text: How can a peace agreement be called a victory when no battle was won?
hook.a: Allah called it a clear victory (48:1): peace opened hearts, and Islam spread faster than ever.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Indeed, We have given you a clear victory' (al-Fath 48:1). إِنَّا فَتَحْنَا لَكَ فَتْحًا مُّبِينًا

starter.q: Which ayah says 'perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you'?
Who escaped and camped by the coast?
What was the first term of the treaty?
Who advised the Prophet ﷺ to shave first?

teach.heading: Surah al-Fath
bullets: 'We have given you a clear victory' (48:1)
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Bukhari and Muslim report the revelation on the way back and Umar's question. Ask: what kind of victory?

teach.heading: Islam spreads in peace
bullets: Letters sent to rulers, including Heraclius
Khalid ibn al-Walid and Amr ibn al-As accepted Islam
teach.note: The scholar az-Zuhri observed that more people entered Islam in the two years after Hudaybiyyah than in all the years before (reported in the seerah). The letter to Heraclius is in Bukhari.

teach.heading: The truce is broken
bullets: The way to Makkah was opened (8 AH)
teach.note: Khuza'ah were allies of the Muslims under the alliance term. Quraysh's support for the attack broke the treaty. Abu Sufyan went to Madinah to try to renew it, without success.

check.q: How was the treaty broken?
options: Quraysh helped their allies attack the Muslims' allies
check.why: Banu Bakr, helped by Quraysh, attacked Khuza'ah. The Muslims kept the treaty; it had not reached ten years; Abu Basir was outside its terms.

teach.heading: Why 'a clear victory'
bullets: Recognition: Quraysh treated Muslims as equals
It opened the way to Makkah
teach.note: Summarise: a diplomatic, moral and spiritual victory before any military one. Link forward to next lesson.

practice.q: Use the chart: by roughly how many times did the number grow from 1,400 to 10,000?
practice.model: I do: divide the new number by the old: 10,000 ÷ 1,400. 1,400 × 7 = 9,800, so it is just over 7 times.

practice.q: Which surah begins 'We have given you a clear victory'?
practice.a: Al-Fath (48)

practice.q: Name one famous Companion who accepted Islam during the truce.
practice.a: Khalid ibn al-Walid or Amr ibn al-As

independent.q: In the portal response box, write a PEEL answer: 'Explain why the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah is called a clear victory.' Give two developed points.
independent.a: Points: peace allowed da'wah and growth (1,400 to 10,000); recognition by Quraysh; opened the way to the conquest; evidence 48:1 and az-Zuhri's observation. Link.
independent.model: Teacher models point 1: 'Point: it was a victory because peace allowed Islam to spread. Evidence: about 1,400 came to Hudaybiyyah, but about 10,000 marched on Makkah two years later. Explain: ...'

independent.q: Extend: why might da'wah succeed more in peace than in war?
independent.a: People can meet, talk and see Muslims' character without fear or hostility.

independent.q: Stretch: what does Hudaybiyyah teach Muslims today about peace?
independent.a: Seeking peaceful solutions can achieve more; Islam values treaties and honest diplomacy (8:61).

exit.q: Which tribe allied to the Muslims was attacked?
Back to our ponder: how is peace a victory?
exit.a: It allowed Islam to spread, won recognition and opened the way to Makkah (48:1).

lessons.homework: Revise the Hudaybiyyah timeline (journey, pledge, terms, Abu Basir, truce broken) for a short quiz in week 5.
lessons.send: SEND: results cards to sort into 'recognition', 'spread', 'strength'. EAL: key word list. Stretch: read the opening of Surah al-Fath (48:1-3) in translation.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: The Prophet as leader and sawm
lessons.title: Forgiveness at the Conquest: mercy in victory
lessons.bigQuestion: Is forgiving someone a sign of weakness or of strength?
objectives: To understand how the Prophet ﷺ showed forgiveness at the Conquest of Makkah and why Islam values it
successCriteria: All: describe how the Prophet ﷺ treated Quraysh after the conquest
Most: give two examples of individuals who were forgiven
Some: explain the difference between forgiveness and allowing injustice
lessons.smsc: Moral: forgiveness and reconciliation

keywords.def: pardoning: letting go of the right to punish
an enemy who was forgiven and became a Muslim
Abu Sufyan's wife, who accepted Islam at the conquest

hook.text: Is forgiving someone a sign of weakness or of strength?
hook.a: Of strength: the Prophet ﷺ forgave when he had full power to punish.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Let them pardon and overlook. Would you not love for Allah to forgive you?' (an-Nur 24:22), and 'We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds' (al-Anbiya 21:107).

starter.q: Which surah begins 'When the victory of Allah has come'?
Name one of the safe places at the conquest.
starter.a: Abu Sufyan's house, one's own home, or al-Masjid al-Haram

starter.q: Which ayah: 'Truth has come and falsehood has vanished'?
Who gave the adhan from the Ka'bah?

teach.heading: What Quraysh had done
bullets: Tortured the weak, such as Bilal
Boycotted the Muslims for three years
Plotted to kill the Prophet ﷺ; fought at Badr, Uhud, the Trench
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. Set the scale of the wrongs so pupils understand the scale of the forgiveness.

teach.heading: The address at the Ka'bah
bullets: He forgave them and let them go free
Seerah reports he quoted Yusuf: 'No blame on you today' (12:92)
teach.note: These words are reported in the seerah (Ibn Ishaq and others) rather than Bukhari or Muslim: say so. The point is secure: Quraysh as a whole were pardoned.

check.q: Why was the forgiveness at Makkah so remarkable?
options: He had full power to punish, yet pardoned
check.why: He held complete power after years of persecution and chose mercy. Quraysh had harmed many; nobody forced him.

teach.heading: Individuals forgiven
teach.note: A very small number were excluded at first for serious crimes; several of them were later forgiven too, such as Ikrimah, who became a strong Muslim. Keep the focus on mercy.

head: Person
What they had done
What happened
rows: Honoured: his house a place of safety
Son of Abu Jahl, fought the Muslims

teach.heading: Forgiveness is not weakness
teach.note: Islam allows just punishment but praises pardon (42:40: whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah). Forgiving does not mean pretending wrong was right, or ignoring safety.

misconception.wrong: Forgiving means you are weak or that the wrong did not matter.
misconception.right: Forgiving is choosing mercy when you could punish; justice still matters, and it takes strength.

practice.q: Explain why forgiving Quraysh was also wise, not only kind.
practice.a: It won hearts: many accepted Islam sincerely, Makkah became peaceful, and revenge would have caused endless feuds.
practice.model: I do: 1) What would revenge cause? More hatred and feuds. 2) What did forgiveness cause? People entered Islam in crowds (110:2). 3) So mercy was both kind and wise.

practice.q: Which ayah asks 'Would you not love for Allah to forgive you?'

independent.q: In the portal response box: 'Forgiveness is a sign of strength, not weakness.' Write a balanced answer with evidence from the conquest and the Qur'an, and a conclusion.
independent.a: Agree: forgave with full power; 24:22, 42:40; won hearts. Other view: justice matters; some crimes need justice; Islam balances both. Conclusion.
independent.model: Teacher models: 'I agree, because the Prophet ﷺ forgave Quraysh when he had complete power over them. Forgiving when you are weak may be necessity, but forgiving when you are strong is a choice ...'

independent.q: Extend: how can you apply this when a friend wrongs you?
independent.a: Pardon, make du'a, talk it through; protect yourself if needed, without revenge.

exit.q: Which enemy's son was forgiven and became a Muslim?
Back to our ponder: weakness or strength?
exit.a: Strength: choosing mercy when you could punish.

lessons.homework: Write about one person you will forgive this week (no names needed) and a du'a you will make for them.
lessons.send: SEND: two-column sort (strength / weakness statements). EAL: argument connectives. Stretch: compare the Prophet's ﷺ words with Yusuf's in 12:92.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: The Prophet as leader and sawm
lessons.title: Leadership of the Prophet ﷺ: consultation and service
lessons.bigQuestion: What makes people WANT to follow a leader, rather than just obey because they have to?
objectives: To understand how the Prophet ﷺ led through consultation and service
successCriteria: All: give two examples of the Prophet ﷺ consulting the Companions
Most: give two examples of the Prophet ﷺ serving others
Some: explain how 3:159 describes his leadership
lessons.crossCurricular: Business (Year 10 option): leadership styles and their effect on a team
lessons.smsc: Social: being a leader who listens and serves

keywords.def: a shepherd or guardian responsible for others

hook.text: What makes people WANT to follow a leader, rather than just obey because they have to?
hook.a: Gentleness, listening, serving alongside them and good character (3:159).

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'By mercy from Allah you were gentle with them; had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you. So pardon them, ask forgiveness for them and consult them in the matter; and when you have decided, rely on Allah' (Al Imran 3:159).

starter.q: Name one person forgiven at the conquest of Makkah.
Which ayah teaches 'pardon and overlook'?
Who advised on the wells at Badr?
Who advised the Prophet ﷺ at Hudaybiyyah to shave first?

teach.heading: Leading by consultation
bullets: Badr: al-Hubab's advice on the wells
Uhud: went out to meet the enemy, as most advised
The Trench: Salman's idea of digging a trench
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. The Trench idea is from the seerah; the others were covered in earlier units. Ash-Shura 42:38 describes believers whose affairs are decided by consultation among them.

teach.heading: Leading by service
bullets: Dug and carried earth at the Trench (Bukhari)
Ate and sat with the poor
teach.note: Aisha said he used to be in the service of his family, and when the time for prayer came he went out to pray (Bukhari). Ask: why does a leader who works alongside people earn respect?

teach.heading: Two kinds of leader
teach.note: Discuss 3:159: gentleness keeps people together.

teach.heading: Every one of you is a shepherd
bullets: Every person is responsible for those in their care
Leadership is a trust (amanah), not a prize
teach.note: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Every one of you is a shepherd and every one of you is responsible for his flock' (Bukhari and Muslim).

check.q: According to 3:159, what happens to followers of a harsh leader?
check.why: Allah says that had he been harsh, they would have scattered. Gentleness keeps people together.

practice.q: Identify consultation or service: a) digging the trench with the Companions b) asking the Companions whether to go out at Uhud c) helping his family at home.
practice.a: a) service b) consultation c) service
practice.model: I do a): 'He physically worked with them, so it is service (khidmah).' Pupils do b) and c).

practice.q: Which ayah says believers decide affairs by consultation?

independent.q: In the portal response box, write a PEEL answer: 'Explain how the Prophet ﷺ led through consultation and service.' Give one developed point for each.
independent.a: Consultation: Badr wells, Uhud, Trench, Umm Salamah; 3:159, 42:38. Service: bricks, Trench digging, family; hadith of Aisha. Link to why people followed him.
independent.model: Teacher models the consultation point: 'Point: the Prophet ﷺ consulted his Companions before big decisions. Evidence: at Badr he accepted al-Hubab's advice about the wells, and Allah told him to "consult them in the matter" (3:159). Explain: ...'

independent.q: Extend: give one way you can follow this leadership in a group task.
independent.a: Ask everyone's ideas before deciding; take on the hardest job yourself.

independent.q: Stretch: why does 3:159 say 'when you have decided, rely on Allah'?
independent.a: Consultation does not replace decision or tawakkul: the leader decides and then trusts Allah.

exit.q: Whose idea was the trench?
Back to our ponder: what makes people want to follow a leader?
exit.a: Gentleness, listening, serving and good character.

lessons.homework: Interview an adult who leads something (a family, a team, a masjid group) about how they make decisions; compare with the Prophet's ﷺ way.
lessons.send: SEND: example cards sorted into consultation and service. EAL: frame 'He consulted when ... He served when ...'. Stretch: read 3:159 in full and annotate.
resources: Pupil PDF worksheet: leadership organiser and PEEL frame

lessons.unit: Spring 1: The Prophet as leader and sawm
lessons.title: Leadership lessons: justice, mercy and keeping promises
lessons.bigQuestion: Should a leader treat their own family exactly the same as everyone else under the rules?
objectives: To understand how justice, mercy and keeping promises made the Prophet ﷺ a model leader
successCriteria: All: give one example each of justice, mercy and keeping promises
Most: support each example with evidence
Some: evaluate which quality matters most in a leader today
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship (PSHE): the rule of law and equality before the law in Britain
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness and trustworthiness

hook.text: Should a leader treat their own family exactly the same as everyone else under the rules?
hook.a: Yes: the Prophet ﷺ said that even if his own daughter Fatimah stole, the law would apply (Bukhari and Muslim).

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'And indeed, you are of a great moral character' (al-Qalam 68:4).

starter.q: Which ayah tells the Prophet ﷺ to consult them?
Finish: 'Every one of you is a ...'
Who was returned to Makkah to keep the treaty?
Which ayah calls the Prophet ﷺ a mercy to the worlds?

teach.heading: Justice: the same law for all
bullets: A noble woman of Makhzum stole
People asked Usamah to plead for her
'Nations before you were destroyed' for favouring the powerful
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. The hadith of the Makhzumi woman is in Bukhari and Muslim. Read the key line from a trusted translation. Ask: why is equality before the law so important?

quote.text: Those before you were destroyed because when a noble person among them stole, they left him, and when a weak person stole, they punished him.
quote.source: The hadith of the Makhzumi woman, Bukhari and Muslim (paraphrased)

teach.heading: Mercy
bullets: Ta'if: refused to destroy its people
Gentle with children and the weak
teach.note: Link back to Year 5 Ta'if and last week's conquest. At-Tawbah 9:128: grievous to him is what you suffer; he is concerned for you, kind and merciful to the believers.

teach.heading: Keeping promises
bullets: Hudaybiyyah: returned Abu Jandal to keep the treaty
Badr: kept a promise Hudhayfah made to Quraysh
Known as al-Amin even before prophethood
teach.note: Muslim reports that Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman and his father were released by Quraysh on a promise not to fight; the Prophet ﷺ told them to keep it: 'We will keep their promise and seek Allah's help against them.'

check.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ say about Fatimah in the hadith of the Makhzumi woman?
options: The law would apply even to her
check.why: He said the law would apply even to his own daughter: no one is above justice.

teach.heading: Which quality matters most?
teach.note: Pupils vote, then justify. There is no single right answer; reward reasoning with evidence.

practice.q: Match each event to a quality: Ta'if; Abu Jandal; the Makhzumi woman.
practice.a: Ta'if: mercy. Abu Jandal: keeping promises. The Makhzumi woman: justice.
practice.model: I do the first: 'At Ta'if he refused to have the people destroyed and hoped for their children: that is mercy (rahmah).'

practice.q: Which ayah praises his great character?

independent.q: In the portal response box: 'Justice is the most important quality in a leader.' Evaluate, using at least three events from the Prophet's ﷺ life, with a conclusion.
independent.a: Argues with evidence: Makhzumi woman (justice), Ta'if and Makkah (mercy), Hudaybiyyah and Hudhayfah (promises); weighs them; justified conclusion.
independent.model: Teacher models the opening: 'Some would agree, because without justice people lose trust in their leader. The Prophet ﷺ showed this when ...'

independent.q: Extend: name a quality from the Prophet's ﷺ leadership you can practise as a form captain or older sibling.
independent.a: For example: treating everyone equally, keeping my word, serving first.

exit.q: The hadith of the Makhzumi woman teaches ...
Back to our ponder: should a leader treat their family the same?
exit.a: Yes: the law applies to everyone, as the Prophet ﷺ said about Fatimah.

lessons.homework: Revise Hudaybiyyah, the conquest and leadership for the short quiz in the sawm lesson next week.
lessons.send: SEND: three quality cards with one event each. EAL: evaluation connectives. Stretch: link to the rule of law in Britain.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: The Prophet as leader and sawm
lessons.title: Sawm: the spirit of fasting and preparing for Ramadan; short quiz
lessons.bigQuestion: Can someone fast all day and still gain nothing from it? How?
objectives: To understand the spiritual purpose of fasting and how to prepare for a meaningful Ramadan
successCriteria: All: explain how fasting builds taqwa
Most: answer the short quiz on Hudaybiyyah, the conquest and sawm
Some: write a realistic Ramadan plan for character, Qur'an and giving
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: self-discipline, gratitude and generosity

keywords.def: awareness of Allah that makes us obey Him
the Night of Power, better than a thousand months (97:3)

hook.text: Can someone fast all day and still gain nothing from it? How?
hook.a: Yes: the Prophet ﷺ said whoever does not leave false speech and acting on it, Allah has no need of his leaving food and drink (Bukhari).

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and hoping for reward, his previous sins will be forgiven' (Bukhari and Muslim).

starter.q: Does eating by mistake break the fast?
Who makes up missed fasts later?
starter.a: The ill and travellers (and others excused for a time)

starter.q: What is fidyah?
starter.a: Feeding a poor person for each day someone cannot fast
options: Feeding a poor person for each day

teach.heading: Fasting builds taqwa
bullets: Purpose: 'so that you may attain taqwa' (2:183)
Obeying Allah when no one sees
Self-control over food, anger and words
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. If someone insults or fights a fasting person, he should say 'I am fasting' (Bukhari and Muslim).

teach.heading: More than food and drink
teach.note: Hadith in Bukhari on false speech. The Prophet ﷺ was the most generous of people, and most generous in Ramadan when Jibril met him to review the Qur'an (Bukhari).

left.title: An empty fast
points: No food, but lying and arguing

teach.heading: Making the most of Ramadan
teach.note: Ramadan begins around the end of this half term (the date depends on the moon sighting). Plans should be small and steady: 'the most beloved deeds to Allah are the most regular, even if small' (Bukhari and Muslim).

check.q: Which is the best Ramadan goal?
options: Read two pages of Qur'an with meaning every day
Read the whole Qur'an on the first day only
Fast but stay up all night gaming
check.why: Small and regular is most beloved to Allah. One huge burst then stopping, or neglecting prayer, misses the spirit.

teach.heading: Short quiz
teach.note: Run the quiz as the independent task. Note the most-missed topics for Spring 2 starters.

practice.q: Turn 'I want a good Ramadan' into a SMART goal for character.
practice.a: For example: 'Each day of Ramadan, when I feel angry I will say "I am fasting" and stay silent, and I will count how often I manage it.'
practice.model: I do: 1) Pick one area: character. 2) Make it specific: anger. 3) Make it measurable: count each day. 4) Make it based on the Sunnah: say 'I am fasting'.

independent.q: Short quiz (Teams Forms, 10 questions): 1) Year of Hudaybiyyah? 2) Ayah of the pledge? 3) One term of the treaty? 4) Who arrived in chains? 5) Ayah 'a clear victory'? 6) Year of the conquest? 7) Ayah recited at the idols? 8) Ayah 'consult them'? 9) Does forgetting break the fast? 10) Who pays fidyah?
independent.a: 1) 6 AH 2) 48:18 3) Any of the four terms 4) Abu Jandal 5) 48:1 6) 8 AH 7) 17:81 8) 3:159 9) No 10) Someone who can never fast
independent.model: Teacher answers a sample question (not in the quiz): 'Who negotiated for Quraysh? Suhayl ibn Amr.'

independent.q: In the portal response box, write your Ramadan plan: one character goal, one Qur'an goal, one act of giving, each specific and realistic.
independent.a: Three SMART goals rooted in the Sunnah.

independent.q: Stretch: explain 'fasting is a shield' in your own words.
independent.a: It protects from sin in this life by training self-control, and from the Fire in the next.

exit.q: What is Laylat al-Qadr better than?
Back to our ponder: how can a fast gain nothing?
exit.a: If the person keeps lying, arguing or doing wrong while fasting.

lessons.homework: Share your Ramadan plan with your family and ask them to help you keep it; review it after the first week of Ramadan.
lessons.send: SEND: quiz read aloud with options. EAL: glossary allowed. Stretch: plan must link each goal to an ayah or hadith.
resources: Teams Forms short quiz (10 questions, in the independent section)

lessons.title: The Farewell Sermon: life, property and the end of riba
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do you think the Prophet ﷺ started his last great sermon with people's lives and property?
objectives: To understand the first messages of the Farewell Sermon about the sanctity of life and property and the end of riba
successCriteria: All: name two rights the sermon protects
Most: explain why the Prophet ﷺ compared them to the sacred day, month and city
Some: explain why riba and blood feuds were ended
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship: rights and the rule of law
lessons.smsc: Moral: sanctity of life and property; Social: justice

keywords.def: interest or usury, forbidden in Islam

hook.text: Why do you think the Prophet ﷺ started his last great sermon with people's lives and property?
hook.a: Because protecting life and property is the basis of a just society.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Allah has permitted trade and has forbidden riba' (al-Baqarah 2:275).

starter.q: Bismillah. 5:3 was revealed at ...
The Farewell Pilgrimage was in ...
'Take your rites from me' refers to ...

teach.heading: Sacred like this day
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah.

quote.text: Your blood and your wealth are sacred to you, like the sacredness of this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this land of yours.

teach.heading: Ending the old ways
bullets: Blood feuds of the time of ignorance are ended
Riba of the time of ignorance is ended
He began with his own family's claims
teach.note: Reported by Muslim in Jabir's long hadith of the Hajj.

teach.heading: Riba in Islam
bullets: Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba (2:275)
Islamic finance shares profit and risk
Interest is taught as knowledge, never to take
teach.note: Standard school riba note: partnership (musharakah) and cost-plus sale (murabahah) instead of interest.

teach.heading: Quick check
teach.note: 30 seconds, then share.

check.q: Why compare life and wealth to the sacred day?
options: To show they must never be violated
check.why: The day, month and city were all sacred; so are a Muslim's life and property.

practice.q: Explain why the Prophet ﷺ ended blood feuds.
practice.a: They caused endless revenge killings; ending them protected life and united the community.
practice.model: Point: ending feuds protected life. Evidence: 'Your blood and your wealth are sacred' (Bukhari and Muslim); feuds of ignorance were ended (Muslim). Explain: revenge passed down generations; the sermon stopped it. Link: justice replaces revenge.

practice.q: Which ayah says trade is permitted and riba forbidden?

independent.q: Sermon notes on the pupil PDF: for each message (life, property, feuds, riba) write the meaning, why it mattered then, and one example of it today.
independent.a: Accurate meanings, context and modern examples (e.g. knife crime, theft, payday loans)
independent.model: Teacher fills 'Life: sacred like the day of Arafah. Then: tribal revenge killings. Today: violence on the streets.'

independent.q: Extend: why start with his own family's claims?
independent.a: To lead by example and show the rule applies to everyone.

independent.q: Stretch: how does Islamic finance avoid riba?
independent.a: Sharing profit and risk (musharakah) or a fixed cost-plus sale (murabahah).

exit.q: Riba is ...
Back to our ponder: why start with life and property?

lessons.title: The Last Day: resurrection, the record, the scales and the Sirat
lessons.bigQuestion: An atom's weight of good will be seen. Does that make small deeds feel more or less important to you?
objectives: To understand the main events of the Day of Judgement and how they show Allah's justice and mercy
successCriteria: All: put the main events of the Last Day in order
Most: explain the scales and the record with evidence
Some: explain how the Last Day shows both justice and mercy
lessons.smsc: Moral: accountability for every deed

hook.text: An atom's weight of good will be seen. Does that make small deeds feel more or less important to you?
hook.a: More: nothing is wasted (az-Zalzalah 99:7-8).

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'And We place the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be treated unjustly at all' (al-Anbiya' 21:47).

starter.q: Bismillah. Barzakh means ...
Which hadith collection reports the questioning about 'this man'?
Name one deed that continues after death.

teach.heading: Events of the Day
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. The order is the general order taught by scholars.

quote.text: So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it.

teach.heading: The record and the Sirat
bullets: Records in the right or left hand
teach.note: The Sirat is described in the long hadith of intercession in Bukhari and Muslim. The record: al-Haqqah 69:19-25.

check.q: Which ayah says no soul will be wronged on the Day?
check.why: 21:47: We place the scales of justice; no soul is wronged at all.

practice.q: Explain the scales with evidence.
practice.a: Deeds are weighed exactly; even an atom's weight is seen (99:7-8); heavy scales lead to a pleasant life (101:6-7)
practice.model: Teacher: 'Belief: deeds are weighed. Evidence: 99:7-8. Meaning: small deeds matter; nothing is lost.'

independent.q: 12-mark style practice in the portal response box (or a Forms long-answer question): 'Belief in the Last Day is the most important belief for making people behave well.' Evaluate (for, against, judgement).
independent.a: For: accountability, scales, record; Against: love of Allah, tawhid and the example of the Prophet ﷺ also motivate; judgement
independent.model: Teacher writes the 'for' point: 'Many Muslims would agree, because knowing every atom of good and evil will be seen (99:7-8) makes people think before acting.'

independent.q: Stretch: what is shafa'ah and what is its condition?
independent.a: Intercession; only by Allah's permission (2:255)

exit.q: Mizan means ...
Back to our ponder: do small deeds matter more now?

keywords.def: trusting Allah after taking the means

hook.text: Two pupils miss a grade by one mark. One says 'it was written, whatever'. The other says 'qaddara Allah' and revises harder. Who has understood qadar?
hook.a: The second: accept the past, take means for the future.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'How wonderful is the affair of the believer, for all of it is good: if good befalls him he is grateful, and if harm befalls him he is patient' (Muslim).

starter.q: Bismillah. Name the four levels of qadr.
'Act, for each is eased' is in ...
81:29: you do not will except that ...

teach.heading: The believer's affair
teach.note: Begin with Bismillah. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'How wonderful is the affair of the believer ...' (Muslim).

teach.heading: Do not say 'if only'
bullets: Seek Allah's help; do not give up
If something happens say: qaddara Allah wa ma sha'a fa'al
teach.note: Muslim. 'If only' opens the door to Shaytan's work.

quote.text: قَدَّرَ اللَّهُ وَمَا شَاءَ فَعَلَ
quote.source: Allah decreed, and what He willed He did (Muslim)

teach.heading: Du'a and effort
bullets: Du'a is part of the decree
Tawakkul: take the means, trust Allah

check.q: Someone misses Fajr and says 'it was decreed'. The correct response is ...
options: We cannot use qadar to excuse sins; repent and set an alarm
Qadar means no one is responsible
check.why: Qadar is not an excuse for sin.

practice.q: Explain the hadith of the believer's affair.
practice.a: Every situation is good for a believer: gratitude in ease, patience in hardship (Muslim)
practice.model: Teacher: 'Good news: shukr, reward. Bad news: sabr, reward. Either way the believer gains.'

independent.q: Response cards on the pupil PDF: six real-life situations (exam result, illness, a win, a loss): write the right words and actions. Then in the portal response box (or a Forms long-answer question) explain how du'a and effort fit with belief in qadar.
independent.a: Correct responses (alhamdulillah, inna lillah, qaddara Allah) and a reasoned paragraph
independent.model: Teacher does card 1: 'Good exam result: say alhamdulillah, thank teachers, do not boast; Muslim hadith: gratitude.'

independent.q: Stretch: why is contentment (ridha) different from not caring?
independent.a: Ridha accepts Allah's choice while still striving and feeling

exit.q: What do we say when harm happens (Muslim)?
exit.a: Qaddara Allah wa ma sha'a fa'al

exit.q: Back to our ponder: who understood qadar?
